title: The Captured Ark Brings Trouble
overview: After the Philistines capture Israel's sacred chest, the ark, their own god topples before it and a deadly sickness follows it from city to city until they want it gone.

parts.label: The ark as a war prize (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The ark was a chest covered in gold that stood for the LORD's presence with Israel, and the Philistines had just taken it in battle. Placing it beside the statue of Dagon, their chief god, most likely displayed it as a trophy, as if to say Dagon had beaten Israel's God.

parts.label: Dagon falls twice (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Two mornings in a row the statue is found face down before the ark, the way a worshipper would lie, and the second time its head and hands lie broken off on the doorway. The writer adds that Dagon's priests still avoided stepping on that doorway in his day; older writers pictured Dagon as half fish, but scholars are unsure what he looked like.

parts.label: Sickness in Ashdod (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: The LORD's "heavy hand" means a crushing blow, here an outbreak of swellings or tumors, and the people of Ashdod connect it with what happened to Dagon. The exact disease is unclear; some scholars suggest a plague, partly because rats are mentioned in the next chapter.

parts.label: Passed from city to city (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: The Philistine rulers move the ark to Gath and then Ekron, two more of their five main cities, but panic, tumors and deaths follow it each time. The story does not soften this: people die, those who live are struck with tumors, and Ekron's cry goes up to heaven as its people demand the ark be sent home.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether to read the fallen statue and the plague as literal events directly caused by God, or as a story shaped mainly to show that Israel's God was not defeated even when Israel was.
think: When something people trusted to protect them clearly fails, why do they so often set it back up rather than rethink it?
